item.title: Rising Refinancing Costs Set to Divide Commercial Property Performance
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Wells Fargo executives say higher interest rates will compress commercial property values at refinancing, though stress has not yet materialized across the portfolio.

The post Rising Refinancing Costs Set to Divide Commercial Property Performance appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Wells Fargo executives told investors Tuesday that rising interest rates will push down commercial real estate valuations as properties refinance, though the bank sees no acute distress yet. Chief Financial Officer Mike Santomassimo said the relationship is straightforward: higher rates mean lower valuations when all other factors remain constant. CEO Charlie Scharf emphasized the bank feels confident about its own commercial real estate portfolio. Wells Fargo shares dropped 3.1% in regular trading following the earnings release.

Santomassimo said property performance will vary widely depending on whether net operating income can absorb higher debt costs during refinancing. Some buildings will handle the transition without issue, while others will face increased financial pressure. The comments come as owners confront refinancing at rates substantially higher than those locked in during the early pandemic years. Recent reporting shows that higher borrowing costs are already forcing buyers to renegotiate purchase prices or walk away from deals that no longer generate acceptable returns.

Wells Fargo’s cautious tone matches broader industry concern about a wave of maturing commercial loans facing costlier debt. Scharf noted that while the bank’s consumer lending businesses continue to grow and customer fundamentals remain solid, underwriting standards now account for an eventual weakening in credit conditions. The bank has not yet observed signs of consumer stress, but executives acknowledged that economic cycles are unavoidable. Property owners with strong cash flow will navigate refinancing more easily than those operating on thin margins or in weaker markets.

San Francisco Business Times
Wells Fargo Exec Warns Higher Interest Rates Will Hurt Commercial Real Estate Valuations. ‘It’s Just Math’

The post Rising Refinancing Costs Set to Divide Commercial Property Performance appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Real Estate Is About to Get Its Own Flood of AI Slop
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Authentic expertise matters more than production volume

The post Real Estate Is About to Get Its Own Flood of AI Slop appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
1 hr 12 min agoOct. 13, 2026 5:17 pm

The volume of video content real estate agents produce is about to increase by an order of magnitude. Content production has always been the constraint. Filming takes time, editing takes more, and both compete directly with the work that actually generates commissions. Ryan Serhant’s new project is the clearest signal yet that the constraint is gone. He has partnered with HeyGen to launch @HeySerhant, a channel publishing original content daily for the next twelve months through an AI avatar built on his likeness and voice. He approves the topics and signs off personally on anything tied to the market. “For an agent, every hour spent filming is an hour you’re not with a client, at a showing or working on the business,” he said, which is the entire argument in one sentence and also why this will not stay confined to one channel.

Agents are already leading into AI content production. NAR’s 2026 Realtors Technology Report found 23 percent of agents using AI daily and another 25 percent weekly, with the share using none of it falling to 21 percent from 32 percent a year earlier. Almost all of that use is content production. Seventy-five percent of AI users write listing descriptions, 56 percent write social posts, and 52 percent draft emails. Fifty-four percent named generative AI for content creation as the thing they most want to add over the next twelve months. Video has been the holdout because video required being on camera, and that requirement has now become optional.

Other industries have already found ways to harness AI content production. Graphite found that roughly half of newly published English-language articles are now primarily AI-generated, up from about ten percent before ChatGPT. Pew Research Center analyzed 490,000 pages from Common Crawl and found 10 percent of its July 2026 sample carried significant signs of AI authorship, against roughly one percent in January 2021, with more than a third of post-2022 pages showing those markers.

But just like every trend, there will be a correctio. Graphite found only about 14 percent of articles surfacing in Google Search were AI-written against 86 percent human, which suggests the ranking systems sorted the problem out well ahead of the people creating it. Google now explicitly demotes what it calls scaled content abuse. Consumer sentiment moved in the same direction. A Fractl survey of 1,008 US consumers found the share saying heavy AI use would reduce their trust in a favorite brand doubled from 20 percent in 2025 to roughly 40 percent in 2026, with only 14 percent saying it would increase trust. A June 2026 Harris Poll found 78 percent of consumers believe AI makes advertising feel less authentic and 63 percent are less likely to buy from a brand using AI-generated ads.

Real estate carries an exposure that general marketing does not, because the product being sold is a person. Agents compete on familiarity and judgment, and content exists to demonstrate both. Serhant acknowledged this directly, calling real estate a trust business and noting that HeyGen builds avatars of the actual user rather than a generic presenter. An avatar of a specific agent saying something generic about interest rates is still generic, and the likeness does not compensate for the content.

That is not an argument for abstaining. Content has been part of the playbook since the first open house flyer, and the agents who built durable businesses on Instagram and YouTube did it through years of consistency rather than individual viral moments. Consistency was always the expensive part, and it is the part this technology genuinely addresses. An agent with real expertise in a specific submarket who has never had the time to communicate it now has a way to do so.

Production cost was never what made content valuable, but it functioned as a filter. The friction of setting up a camera forced a moment of deciding whether there was anything worth recording. Removing that friction increases output but could lower the value. What becomes scarce is not production but the value of the content itself. A point of view. Specific knowledge about a specific market. Something that could not have been generated from the prompt “post about the housing market.” The ability to publish daily is about to become universal. The reason to watch will not be.

The post Real Estate Is About to Get Its Own Flood of AI Slop appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Condo Buyers Fund Construction With Bonds in Beverly Hills Tower Deal
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A London developer is raising over $1.6 billion from condo buyers through subordinated bonds to finance its $10 billion Beverly Hills project.

The post Condo Buyers Fund Construction With Bonds in Beverly Hills Tower Deal appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Cain, a London-based investment firm, is raising capital for its $10 billion One Beverly Hills project by selling bonds to the same buyers purchasing its condos. Condo purchasers have already provided around $350 million through what Cain calls Founder Bonds, which pay a 5 percent return and are typically worth 30 percent of the purchase price. The developer aims to raise more than $1.6 billion through the program. All buyers so far have agreed to participate, though the program is voluntary.

The bonds are subordinate to a $2.8 billion senior loan led by J.P. Morgan and a $1.5 billion mezzanine loan from VICI Properties, putting buyers at risk if the project fails to complete. California law limits developer deposits to 3 percent of purchase price and bars using those funds for construction, but those restrictions do not apply to the bonds. The 5 percent return now trails the 10-year Treasury yield, which recently exceeded 5.3 percent. David Reiss, a professor at Cornell Law School, said buyers are accepting a large amount of risk for a small return, though wealthy purchasers may be better positioned to absorb potential losses.

One Beverly Hills, scheduled for completion in 2029 on 17.5 acres, will include Aman-operated condos starting at $15 million, hotel suites, high-end retail, and botanical gardens. Recent sales have exceeded $7,000 per square foot, and one penthouse reserved in July would sell for $200 million. More than $1 billion in units are under contract or reserved. Cain says it has the funds to complete the project without the bonds, but the buyer financing would replace some of its equity commitment.

Los Angeles condo sales through August were the lowest on record since 2012, according to Redfin, and several recent luxury condo projects have ended in developer defaults. Michael Shvo defaulted on a $200 million loan at the Beverly Hills Mandarin Oriental in 2024 and sold remaining units in bulk the following year. Brokers say the ultraluxury market above $10 million attracts different buyers seeking lock-and-leave flexibility, and Beverly Hills has continued to perform even as other parts of the city have declined.

The Wall Street Journal
The Luxury Beverly Hills Condo Project Borrowing Money From Its Future Residents

item.title: The Questions Real Estate Organizations Should Answer Before Deploying AI
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Studio
item.description:
Real estate firms can prepare for AI success by defining outcomes, auditing data, strengthening governance, and building flexible integrations.

The post The Questions Real Estate Organizations Should Answer Before Deploying AI appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Every real estate organization might not be adopting AI, but they’re at least thinking about it. With all of the media noise about AI transformation and the inevitable questions from investors and advisors, it is hard for real estate organizations not to have a bit of FOMO. Some executives want to jump into action and not get stuck too long thinking about how to actually deploy it. The truth is, the “thinking about it” stage is actually very important. Assessing an organization’s AI readiness requires answering hard questions about a business’s operations, its data structure, and its strategic direction.

To start, you’ve got to know what problems you’re actually trying to solve. This is where many development teams get tripped up, according to Thomas Mackean, Digital Strategy Expert at JLL. “I am often telling our clients AI features age. Outcomes don’t. Buy the second one,” he says. “The clients who get real value from AI didn’t set out to buy AI – they set out to fix an outcome, and using AI turned out to be the best way to get the job done”:  

According to Mackean, starting with the outcome, rather than with the technology itself, forces the right questions. What does success mean? Who will be using it? How can the process be simplified? This outcome-first approach shapes the rest of the process.

Once you know the outcome, you can audit the data that will feed the decision and apply the proper governance. In large real estate organizations, different teams work with different clients, assets, and tenants, all of whom have legitimate expectations about how their information is handled. “Sometimes you have specific functions that need certain data, but you don’t want them to have access to everything,” Mackean says. “By segregating agents, you can make sure they only have access to certain information. You want AI to be trained, but you don’t want it to learn across different clients.” In other words, implementing the right guardrails early on can prevent access to sensitive data while recording a living history of who has accessed what.

Integration is the next consideration. Most real estate tech stacks are a collection of platforms built independently and connected imperfectly. Property management systems, lease management platforms, CRMs, and market data providers all hold information that AI needs, and getting them to share it reliably takes ongoing work rather than a one-time setup. “‘It worked in the pilot’ isn’t a readiness claim. What’s your plan for month six, after the model, the data and the portfolio have all moved?”  Mackean noted. 

An integration or model that works today can break quietly following an update that changes how data is structured or interpreted. “Sometimes nobody notices until an AI output starts degrading in ways that are hard to trace. One example was a client with an office utilisation agent that over a few weeks showed an unexplained increase in utilisation across all buildings by 15% after a change in hybrid-work policy that should have reduced utilisation. After we investigated we saw it was due to an upgraded badging system for security reasons that had more advanced tailgating logic, rollout of additional wifi access points from totally independent workstreams but had significant impacts for the company’s portfolio strategy. “

Because the models themselves are changing so quickly, it also makes sense to build integrations with more than one of the major AI providers. The models available today are considerably more capable than those from two years ago, and that trajectory is not slowing. “Avoid lock-in with a specific vendor or partner because it helps you stay flexible as the models change,” Mackean said. An architecture that lets you swap the underlying model without rebuilding everything around it costs little to maintain and is worth a lot when the next generation arrives.

Some thought also needs to be put into which models are best for which tasks and how advanced a model the task really needs. Models range from lightweight and cheap to sophisticated and expensive, and using the top tier for everything gets costly fast. “If you are not careful you can find that 90 percent of staff are using the highest level of AI, costing significant sums of money, on tasks where it might not be needed,” Mackean said. Deciding in advance which workflows warrant which model tier, and giving staff clear guidance on that, keeps costs manageable as usage scales.

All of this work happens before a single AI tool goes live, which is exactly the point. The readiness gap is not a technology problem, and it does not close on its own. It closes when an organization has done the work of defining outcomes clearly, auditing its data honestly, mapping the integrations that will need ongoing attention, and building in the flexibility to adapt as the models keep improving. That work is difficult and time consuming, particularly for organizations that have never had to think about their operations at this level of granularity. This is why a growing number of real estate companies are bringing in outside advisors to help them assess where they actually stand before committing to a deployment path. 

So as tempting as it is to be one of those companies “actually integrating AI,” there is real value in taking the “thinking about it” stage seriously. The organizations that spend that time productively, applying the right framework and asking the uncomfortable questions early, are the ones whose pilots produce results worth scaling. The ones that skip it tend to discover the gap later, after the budget has been spent.

The post The Questions Real Estate Organizations Should Answer Before Deploying AI appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: DSCR Loans Pour Capital Into Distressed Urban Neighborhoods Left Behind by Banks
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
DSCR loans approve investors on rental income, not personal finances, flooding capital into East Cleveland, Baltimore, Detroit, and Memphis—but fraud risks loom.

The post DSCR Loans Pour Capital Into Distressed Urban Neighborhoods Left Behind by Banks appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Debt-service coverage ratio loans, introduced in the mid-2010s, approve borrowers based on a property’s rental income potential rather than the investor’s personal finances. Private lenders have deployed these mortgages across East Cleveland, Indianapolis, Baltimore, Detroit, and Memphis, enabling investors to buy and rehabilitate vacant properties in neighborhoods that traditional banks have avoided since the Great Depression-era redlining. Borrowers often provide no proof of personal income. Investors use short-term construction loans to acquire and fix properties, then refinance into 30-year DSCR mortgages if they cannot sell, converting to landlords in markets where rental demand far exceeds buyer demand.

Baltimore has cut its vacant building count by 30% since 2019, driven almost entirely by private capital flowing through DSCR products, according to the city’s former housing commissioner Michael Braverman. Detroit and Cleveland have posted similar vacancy reductions. In the ten most vacant ZIP codes of Cleveland, Baltimore, Detroit, and Memphis, flipping activity has outpaced wealthier neighborhoods since DSCR loans gained traction. Investors cite pricing as the draw: one Florida-based investor reported paying no more than $24,000 for a property around Cleveland, a fraction of costs in higher-priced markets.

Lax underwriting and minimal due diligence have attracted fraud in Baltimore and Philadelphia. A group of New York investors allegedly inflated property values to extract cash on hundreds of Baltimore vacants with minimal improvements, triggering defaults and foreclosures. A similar scheme collapsed in Philadelphia earlier this year. Private lending in Baltimore dropped 40% this year compared to last, and Philadelphia lending fell 19% over the 90 days ended September 11, according to Forecasa. Some lenders have exited both markets entirely.

Memphis investor Raymond Porter bought an abandoned Orange Mound home for $79,000, spent $20,000 on rehabilitation, and refinanced with a $110,000 DSCR mortgage to recoup costs and fund additional acquisitions. He rents the property for $1,400 per month. Orange Mound, believed to be the first U.S. neighborhood built for and by formerly enslaved people, has seen investors renovate vacants alongside community cleanups and returning former residents. Philadelphia investor Tabitha Giddens described the DSCR process as requiring far less paperwork than conventional mortgages, enabling her to hold a rehabbed West Philadelphia property as a rental.

The Wall Street Journal
A New Type of Mortgage Is Reviving Long Abandoned Neighborhoods

The post DSCR Loans Pour Capital Into Distressed Urban Neighborhoods Left Behind by Banks appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: The Legal Challenge That Forced the SEC to Reconsider Its Climate Rules
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
The SEC moves to rescind its 2024 climate disclosure rules, reigniting debate over agency authority, investor needs, and corporate reporting.

The post The Legal Challenge That Forced the SEC to Reconsider Its Climate Rules appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted climate disclosure rules in March of 2024 by a three-to-two vote, following two years of rulemaking and more than 20,000 public comments. Public companies would have been required to report greenhouse gas emissions, describe climate-related business risks on a forward-looking basis, and detail whatever steps they were taking to mitigate those risks.

The rules never took effect. Legal challenges arrived almost immediately. The SEC never implemented the rules and on June 3 the Commission published a proposal to rescind the framework in its entirety. 

The SEC’s stated reasoning covers both authority and policy. The proposal says the rules exceed the scope of the agency’s statutory authority, and adds that even if the authority existed, the rules impose substantial costs on public companies and their shareholders that are not justified by the informational benefits, stray well beyond the policy concerns of the federal securities laws, and conflict with the Commission’s objectives around capital formation.

For the organizations that brought the challenge, a withdrawal on policy grounds is not sufficient.

The New Civil Liberties Alliance represents the National Center for Public Policy Research in National Center for Public Policy Research v. SEC, a case that prompted the Commission to revisit the rules. Both organizations filed comments urging the SEC to rescind and to acknowledge that it lacked statutory authority from the beginning.

“The SEC was given broad authority to regulate the stock market but it was never authorized to be an environmental regulator,” said Alana Black, Senior Litigation Counsel at NCLA. “We have another authority for that, the EPA.”

The statutory argument turns on language written in response to the Crash of 1929. The securities laws authorize the SEC to require disclosure of business and financial information necessary or appropriate in the public interest or for the protection of investors. NCLA’s position is that climate information falls outside that grant, and that reading it otherwise stretches the statute past what Congress wrote.

Two recent developments strengthen that argument considerably. The Supreme Court’s Major Questions Doctrine holds that agencies need clear congressional authorization before taking actions of major economic and political significance, and climate disclosure requirements for every public company in the country would seem to qualify. Congress has considered climate disclosure legislation repeatedly and never passed it. Separately, NCLA’s win in Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce ended Chevron deference, which means courts may no longer defer to an agency’s own interpretation of an ambiguous statute. An expansive reading of the Securities Act would have to persuade a judge on its merits.

Black said the organization deliberately narrowed its focus to the authority question rather than arguing the merits of the policy.

“There are certainly good policy arguments against this rule but we wanted to focus on the authority,” she said. “It is a huge burden to make these companies comply, so we need to know that the SEC is allowed to force companies to do things like this.”

A rescission grounded in policy can be reversed by a future Commission with different policy preferences. A rescission that concedes the agency never had authority is considerably harder to undo, because the next Commission would have to explain what changed about the statute.

That durability question is the reason the comments emphasize it, and Black expects the political window to close quickly.

“I would be shocked if we don’t get a rule change before the next presidential election,” she said.

NCLA’s broader project is constraining administrative agencies rather than opposing any particular regulation. The organization previously led the successful challenge to the SEC’s Nasdaq board diversity rules, and it argues the climate rules share the same defect.

“We want the SEC to not only revoke the rules but to do it in a way that acknowledges that the rules were outside the authority in the beginning,” Black said.

The opposing position, advanced by institutional investors, state pension funds, and sustainability-focused asset managers, is that climate exposure is financial information and that existing materiality standards have not produced consistent or comparable reporting. Supporters of the 2024 rules argued that investors managing long-duration portfolios need standardized emissions and physical risk data to price assets, and that voluntary frameworks have produced disclosure too varied to compare across companies. Several SEC commissioners made versions of that argument when the rules passed.

If the rules are dropped, publicly traded REITs would lose a federal reporting obligation that never actually took effect, but the other sources of disclosure pressure remain. California’s climate disclosure laws apply to companies doing business in the state above certain revenue thresholds regardless of what the SEC does. The EU’s sustainability reporting directive reaches companies with European operations. Lenders increasingly ask for emissions and physical risk data as part of underwriting, and large institutional investors have their own reporting requirements that flow through to the assets they hold.

Local building performance standards operate on an entirely separate track. New York’s Local Law 97 and comparable ordinances in Boston, Denver, Seattle, and a growing list of other cities impose emissions caps on buildings directly, with penalties that do not depend on any federal framework.

What the SEC proceeding will settle is whether the federal securities regulator can require this category of disclosure at all. The answer shapes what any future Commission can attempt, which is why both sides are treating a rule that never took effect as worth the fight.

The post The Legal Challenge That Forced the SEC to Reconsider Its Climate Rules appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: European Landlords Exit Prime Office Holdings as Rate Outlook Darkens
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Major European landlords including Blackstone and Commerz Real are marketing office assets as bond yields reach multi-decade highs and redemption pressure mounts.

The post European Landlords Exit Prime Office Holdings as Rate Outlook Darkens appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Blackstone is marketing a pair of vacant Paris office buildings it developed near Porte de la Chapelle, roughly six years after completion. BNP Paribas provided a €100 million loan for the €180 million project, later extending the debt for three years in 2023. Blackstone has written off its equity and the sale is proceeding with lender consent. Separately, Commerz Real Fund Management appointed Newmark to sell Etoile Saint Honoré, a central Paris office valued at roughly €500 million, while CPI Property Group’s Immofinanz unit is marketing the Spire tower in Warsaw.

Commerz Real’s HausInvest fund recorded more than €600 million in redemptions in the first seven months of 2024, with full-year outflows expected to reach €900 million. German open-ended real estate funds have faced persistent investor withdrawals as clients anticipate further valuation declines. CPI Property Group is selling to reduce leverage ratios that have expanded as property values fell; the company sold a London office development to the Perrodo family earlier this year. JPMorgan Asset Management is also preparing to market a Paris office leased to Barclays for about €250 million.

Government bond yields across major European markets hit multi-decade highs as 42,000 attendees gathered at the Expo Real conference in Munich this week. Some investors have grown impatient waiting for better market conditions; others face loan maturity deadlines or redemption pressure. Rents for top-tier buildings continue to rise, offering a bull case for buyers willing to accept higher financing costs. Brokers say investors now view European real estate primarily as an income and income growth strategy rather than a capital appreciation bet.

Bloomberg
Spate of European Office Sales Shows Fading Hope of Better Times

The post European Landlords Exit Prime Office Holdings as Rate Outlook Darkens appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Why Over 90% of Real Estate AI Pilots Fall Short of Their Goals
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Why do commercial real estate AI pilots fail? Explore how data quality, verification costs, domain models, and workflows determine success.

The post Why Over 90% of Real Estate AI Pilots Fall Short of Their Goals appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The speed of AI adoption in commercial real estate has been remarkable by any measure. JLL’s 2025 Global Real Estate Technology Survey, which gathered responses from more than 1,000 senior CRE decision-makers across 16 markets, found that the share of teams piloting real estate AI jumped from under 5% to 92% in three years. Occupiers are running an average of five real estate AI pilots simultaneously across roughly 27 identified use cases. Technology budgets have been reorganized around AI initiatives, with the top five spending priorities all tied to implementing AI in commercial real estate or preparing for its impact.

The results have not kept pace with the enthusiasm. Only 5% of organizations report having achieved most of their program goals. The rest are still experimenting, still evaluating, or quietly shelving projects that never produced what the business case promised. The gap is rarely about whether AI can perform a task. It is about what happens after a pilot works, turning a promising proof of concept into a reliable, scalable, and economically viable production workflow. That gap is where the real failure patterns repeat, across companies, property types, and vendors.

Before any of that gets diagnosed, most teams skip a step, establishing a baseline. Without a clear read on current cost, turnaround time, accuracy, manual effort, and exception rates, it is hard to prove a pilot moved the needle, let alone build the case to scale it. That baseline should exist before the technology conversation starts, and it is the benchmark every failure pattern below gets measured against.

Real Estate Data Quality Can Make or Break an AI Pilot

The most frequent point of failure is not the model. It is what the model is reading.

“One of the biggest reasons that AI pilots fail is inaccurate data,” said Snehal Joshi, Head of Data Solutions at Hitech i2i. “Many solutions are not able to produce the level of accuracy that they claim, when this happens there will always be disappointment.”

The JLL data supports that diagnosis. More than 60% of companies must address fundamental technology issues such as duplicated functionality or dormant systems before they can fully leverage AI, and 81% report at least three existing systems that are not generating expected results. Those conditions do not disappear when an AI tool is layered on top of them. They propagate.

A pilot designed to prove that AI can extract data from property records will produce output quality that reflects the source material. When the inputs are inconsistent, incomplete, or structured differently across jurisdictions, the accuracy falls below what was promised in the demo, and the project loses credibility with the stakeholders who approved it.

Knowing When AI Is Wrong Matters More Than Being Right

Every AI system produces errors at some rate. That is documented, expected, and manageable. What determines whether a pilot survives is whether the system can identify which outputs are likely to be wrong.

“Some models will tell you that a certain amount of its answers are inaccurate but for it to be useful it has to tell you when of the values are the ones you have to check,” Joshi said.

An aggregate accuracy rate is not actionable. A model reporting 94% accuracy across a batch of lease abstractions tells a reviewer nothing about which 6% require attention, which means either every output gets reviewed or none of them do. Neither option works. Reviewing everything eliminates the efficiency gain. Reviewing nothing exposes the organization to errors in financial models, title work, and compliance filings.

When Verification Costs More Than the Manual Process

The verification problem is where a surprising number of pilots die on economics rather than performance.

“Some of the AI solutions don’t provide enough savings compared to the manual process and once you add in double-checking the model it might even cost more,” Joshi said.

This is the calculation that rarely appears in a pilot proposal. A tool that processes documents faster than a human still requires someone to confirm the results, and if that confirmation takes nearly as long as the original work, the net savings approach zero. Add the cost of the software itself and the implementation effort, and the pilot ends up demonstrating that the old process was cheaper.

Budget pressure makes this worse. JLL found that 65% of organizations have experienced CRE tech budget constraints over the past two years, and that ROI expectations have tightened, requiring more extensive business case development before approval. A pilot that cannot show clear savings does not get funded for a second phase.

Confidence Scoring Turns Verification Into an Exception Queue

One practical way to solve the verification problem is field-level confidence scoring, paired with validation rules and cross-checks. Running multiple models against the same document set and flagging where they diverge is one input into that score, not the whole architecture.

When two independently trained systems produce the same value, confidence in that value is considerably higher than when either produces it alone. When they disagree, that disagreement becomes the review queue. Instead of examining everything, reviewers examine the specific fields where the models could not reach the same conclusion.

Over time, that process generates something more valuable than the individual corrections.

“You can also create a confidence score at the value level and then benchmark those scores,” Joshi said. “Over time you can start to not check data with a high enough score.”

The sample size accumulated through parallel processing allows an organization to calibrate its thresholds empirically rather than by guesswork. If values scoring above a certain level have proven accurate across thousands of documents, those values can pass through without review. The verification burden shrinks as the evidence base grows, which is what turns a pilot’s economics from marginal into compelling.

Generic Models Do Not Understand Real Estate Documents

The choice of model also affects how often the verification problem arises in the first place.

“Most of the models are generic, they are more likely they will hallucinate at some point,” Joshi said. “We have models specific for real estate documents to fine tune the model so it can really understand the nuances.”

Subdivision is a useful illustration. A property record may present what looks like a single property, and a generic model reading it will extract it as one. A model trained on real estate documents should recognize from context that the property has been divided into multiple parcels, each with its own legal description, its own tax identifier, and potentially its own ownership. Missing that distinction produces a record that is confidently wrong in a way that is difficult to catch downstream, because nothing about the extracted output signals that anything was missed.

Production systems need more than a capable model. They need domain context, real-estate-specific evaluation, validation rules, and training against actual edge cases like this one, built from the document types, terminology, and structural conventions real estate records actually use.

Production AI Requires an Operating Model, Not Just Software

The last failure pattern is organizational rather than technical. Companies treat an AI deployment as a product purchase when it functions more like an ongoing service relationship.

“Most solutions are only offering the tech but the service that goes along with the tech is so important,” Joshi said. “What most people want is an end-to-end solution, the tech and the human in the loop.”

The comparison to SaaS is instructive. Enterprise software purchases come with implementation support, configuration assistance, training, and ongoing account management, because the industry learned that shipping a login and walking away produces low adoption and high churn. AI deployments carry all of those requirements and add several more. Models need monitoring. Confidence thresholds need recalibration as document mixes change. Exception handling requires people who understand both the technology and the underlying real estate context.

JLL found that only 33% of the workforce feels adequately trained on AI, and that 70% of occupiers use multiple sourcing strategies including external partnerships to fill capability gaps. Organizations that buy the technology without the supporting service end up staffing those functions internally, usually without having budgeted for them.

What the Successful Pilots Have in Common

The 5% that reach their goals are not working with fundamentally better models. They are working with better preparation.

They have cleaned and structured the data before the pilot begins rather than expecting the AI to compensate for what is missing. They have built verification into the workflow through confidence scoring rather than bolting it on afterward. They have selected models suited to the documents they actually process. And they have treated the vendor relationship as ongoing rather than transactional, with support that extends past implementation into operation.

Before scaling a real estate AI pilot, leaders should be able to answer five questions. Can we measure the baseline? Can we trust the output? Can we identify exceptions efficiently? Does the economics still work after human review? Can the solution operate reliably within the production workflow?

None of that is glamorous, and none of it appears in a product demonstration. It is the difference between a pilot that produces a presentation and one that produces a process the organization keeps using after the pilot period ends. The expectations the real estate industry has placed on AI are not unreasonable. Meeting them mostly depends on work that happens before the technology ever gets switched on.

The post Why Over 90% of Real Estate AI Pilots Fall Short of Their Goals appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Dear CRE Brokers, Stop Making Bad Software Work
item.dc:creator: Aaron Aziz
item.description:
Commercial real estate brokers often force ill-fitting CRM software to work. Learn how to audit workflows and choose tools built for complex CRE deals.

The post Dear CRE Brokers, Stop Making Bad Software Work appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The best brokers I know all have the same strange habit: they can make bad software work. Give a top producer a CRM built for residential agents, or a platform built for landlords, and they’ll bend it, patch it, and run their whole business through it without complaining. It looks like a strength. It’s the reason our industry keeps buying tools that were never built for us. The problem never gets fixed, because the best of us are too good at dealing with whatever gets put in front of us.

Here’s the simple fact that habit hides: almost every tool a commercial broker uses was designed for someone whose job isn’t ours. The CRMs most of us start with were built for residential agents or sales teams. They assume a deal is fast, has one counterparty, and moves in a straight line to a close. The CRE tools built on top of them mostly just bolt real estate features onto that same logic. None of it was built around what we actually do: a months-long negotiation between four parties over free rent, TI, escalations, and options. That’s not a discipline problem. It’s a design problem. And after more than a decade leasing space in New York, I’ve learned you must break the habit on purpose. Here’s what I have found to work.

Start by figuring out where your deals actually live. Before you look at any new tool, spend one honest week paying attention. Every time you need something about an active deal, write down where you found it. The CRM? A spreadsheet? An email thread? A text? Your own head? Most brokers who do this find the same thing. The system they pay for holds names and addresses. Everything that decides whether a deal closes — whose turn it is, what the landlord will really take, why the tenant rep went quiet — lives somewhere else. That list is what you’re shopping for. Not features. A home for the stuff currently living in your head.

Next, look hard at your workarounds. Every spreadsheet you keep next to your CRM is proof the CRM failed you. Write them down. The commission tracker you keep separately. The deal-status column your software has no field for. The follow-up reminders you run through your calendar because the CRM’s reminders don’t match how deals stop and start. Once you can name your workarounds, you can walk into a demo with a real test instead of nodding along at a feature tour.

At the demo, ask one question before anything else: who were your first hundred customers? Feature lists all sound the same on a sales call. Where the product came from does not. If the honest answer is residential teams, or software sales departments, or big landlords, now you know whose business the product was really built for. And to be fair, there’s serious software in this industry. Some of it organized a huge part of commercial real estate over a decade ago, and it’s good at what it does. But a lot of the best CRE tech was built for the owner and the asset manager looking down at a portfolio. In those systems, the broker isn’t the customer. The broker is a data source, filling in a report someone else reads. That’s not a knock. It’s a fit question. And the vendor’s origin story answers it faster than their feature list ever will.

Then put the demo through a real stress test. Every vendor shows you the happy path. Lead comes in, stages move, deal closes. That’s not our business. Our deals stall, restart, and break in ways no pipeline was drawn for. They sit in attorney review for weeks. They go quiet and come back to life. They fall apart at the finish line over a clause nobody saw coming. Pick one of yours that did, and ask the salesperson to walk you through exactly how their system would have tracked it, step by step. Watch how fast the demo slows down. If the salesperson has to improvise, the software will make you improvise too, every single day.

Last, look at what this habit costs the whole firm, not just your desk. I’ve watched good agents lose deals for reasons that had nothing to do with skill. They lost track of whose turn it was. A strong lead emailed in and never got entered, because something “more important” hit at the same moment. I’ve seen brokers who couldn’t capture big parts of their own deals because the software had nowhere to put them. None of those deals died over price or terms. They died over tracking. Now multiply that across a whole shop. Every agent keeping private spreadsheets. Deal data scattered across files nobody else can see. The firm can’t even look at its own pipeline. In a business where a great year and a flat year come down to a handful of deals, “good enough” software quietly takes a cut of every one. If you run a team, do the one-week audit together. The patterns across five agents’ workarounds are your firm’s real requirements, written by the people living in the tools every day.

I finally got tired enough of bending borrowed tools that I partnered with a developer and built one around how the business actually flows called Leasync. It may not be the right fit for every broker, but it exists because I couldn’t find a platform built just for brokers, and I knew one needed to exist.

So next time someone demos a platform for you, don’t ask whether you can make it work. You’re a broker. You can make anything work. That’s the trap. “I made it work” is how you end up a year deep in software that was never built for you. Figure out where your deals actually live. Turn your workarounds into a shopping list. Ask who it was built for. Put it through a real stress test. Then decide. The habit that makes you great at closing is the same one that keeps you loyal to tools that fight you. Breaking it starts with refusing to be impressed by how well you can cope.

item.title: Federal Probe Challenges Race-Based Mortgage Programs at Major Lender
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
HUD opens probe into Wells Fargo's race-based mortgage programs, questioning whether efforts to boost Black homeownership violated fair-lending laws.

The post Federal Probe Challenges Race-Based Mortgage Programs at Major Lender appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Housing and Urban Development opened an investigation into Wells Fargo’s programs designed to increase Black homeownership, questioning whether the bank violated fair-lending laws by offering products or terms based on race. HUD sent a letter to CEO Charlie Scharf on Wednesday stating the agency would examine whether the bank engaged in illegal “sorting” of homeowners. Secretary Scott Turner said HUD is reviewing similar initiatives at other banks.

Wells Fargo committed $60 billion in 2017 to help add 250,000 Black homeowners by 2027, then expanded the program in 2022 to refinance minority homes using its own capital. The bank scaled back its mortgage business broadly in early 2023 but maintained its racial equity pledge. By late 2023, Wells Fargo had achieved about 40 percent of its initial lending commitment and refinanced roughly 5,100 customers with average monthly savings of $100. The bank has since removed its 2023 racial-equity assessment from its website.

The investigation reflects a broader shift in how the administration views programs launched or expanded after 2020, when companies responded to social unrest and investor pressure. IBM and Deloitte paid multimillion-dollar fines last year to settle claims they defrauded the government by considering diversity in hiring and promotion decisions. Black homeownership stood at 46 percent in 2024, compared with 73 percent for white households, according to Pew Research Center.
